chapter.title: Walking the site: reading what got built

cards.body:
Claude just built your app, and the folder has 9 files in it. Which one do you open to change a button's colour?

Walk it like a homeowner on a site visit. Every house has walls, paint, wiring and a stack of paperwork, and **the main files in a small web app usually fall into the same 4 kinds**, plus a few extras like backend or setup files.
cards.simpler: Claude just built your app. The folder has 9 files in it. Which one do you open to change the colour of a button? Look around like a homeowner visiting a building site. Every house has walls, paint, wiring and a pile of paperwork. In the same way, **the main files in a small web app usually come in 4 kinds**, plus a few extras.

cards.prompt: Your quiz app works, but the Start button is a sad grey and you want it green. In the house, that's a paint job. Which file holds the paint?

whyNot.a: That's the walls, not the paint: the page file says a button exists, not what colour it is.
whyNot.c: That's the paperwork, not the paint: the settings file lists the parts your app uses.

cards.reteach: Each file has one job, like each trade on a building site. The page file decides what's there. The styling file decides how it looks, and colour is a looks question.

cards.title: Walls and paint
cards.body:
The *page* file, often called index.html in a plain web app, is the walls and rooms. It says what exists: a heading here, a text box there, a button under it. *HTML* is just the language pages are written in. If your app uses React, the walls live in .jsx or .tsx files inside src/, and index.html is just the front door.

The *styling* file, usually ending in .css, is the paint, the tiles, the light fittings. Colours, sizes, fonts, spacing. **The page says what's there; the styling says how it looks.**

You'd think one file would do both. Keeping them apart means you can repaint the whole house without moving a single wall.
cards.simpler: The page file, often called index.html, is the walls and rooms. It says what is there: a heading, a text box, a button below it. HTML is the language pages are written in. If your app uses React, the walls are in .jsx or .tsx files inside src/, and index.html is just the front door. The styling file, ending in .css, is the paint. It sets colours, sizes, fonts and spacing. **The page says what's there; the styling says how it looks.** Keeping them apart means you can repaint the whole house without moving a wall.

cards.title: Maya's green button
cards.body:
Maya built a tip calculator on Sunday and wanted the Calculate button green. Maya opened index.html and scrolled for twenty minutes, hunting for the word grey. It wasn't there, because you don't find paint by staring at walls.

So Maya typed: "Which file sets the colour of the Calculate button? Show me the line." Claude pointed to styles.css, line 14. One change, one refresh, green.
cards.simpler: Maya built a tip calculator on Sunday and wanted the Calculate button to be green. Maya opened index.html and scrolled for twenty minutes, looking for the word grey. It wasn't there. You don't find paint by staring at walls. So Maya typed a question for Claude: "**Which file sets the colour of the Calculate button? Show me the line.**" Claude pointed to styles.css, line 14. One change, one refresh, and the button was green.

cards.prompt: Ben's to-do app has an Add button. Ben wants a second button, Clear all, sitting right under it. Which file gets the new button?

options.text: styles.css, because buttons are something you see
the page file (index.html or a .tsx file), because a new button is a new thing on the page
package.json, because it's a new part

whyNot.a: That's the paint, not the walls: styling can make the button pretty, but only once the page says it exists.
whyNot.c: That's the paperwork, not the walls: the parts list is for downloaded parts, not buttons.

cards.reteach: Ask yourself: am I adding a thing, or changing how a thing looks? Adding a thing is building a wall, so it goes in the page file. Changing its looks is paint, so it goes in styling.

cards.title: Wiring and paperwork
cards.body:
The *logic* file, usually ending in .js (*JavaScript*, the language that makes pages do things), is the wiring. You click a button, and the logic decides what happens: work out the tip, save the item, show a message.

Many projects also have a *settings* file, package.json, the clipboard in the site office: the list of parts your app uses and the commands that start it. Next to it usually sits node_modules, the delivered parts themselves, often thousands of files.

Lost? Point at one file and ask: **"In plain words, what does this file do, and which file would I change to make X?"**
cards.simpler: The logic file, usually ending in .js, is the wiring. JavaScript makes pages do things. Click a button, and the logic decides what happens. Many projects also have a settings file, package.json, the site clipboard: the parts your app uses and the commands that start it. Beside it, node_modules usually holds the delivered parts, often thousands of files. Lost? Point at one file and ask: **"In plain words, what does this file do, and which file would I change to make X?"**

cards.body: On day three Jo opened node_modules, saw folder after folder of code, and shut the laptop, sure the app was beyond them. But that folder is the lumber delivery, not the house. A tool called npm fetched it, often at Claude's request, and nobody reads it. If a file lives inside node_modules, skip it. Your app is the handful of files outside it.
cards.simpler: On day three, Jo opened node_modules. Jo saw folder after folder of code, shut the laptop, and felt sure the app was too hard for them. But that folder is the lumber delivery, not the house. A tool called npm fetched it, often because Claude asked it to, and nobody reads it. **If a file lives inside node_modules, skip it.** Your app is the few files outside it.

cards.prompt: Pick the true sentence about your project folder.

options.text: index.html makes the button do something when you click it
package.json lists the parts and start commands; node_modules holds the parts, and you can skip it
styles.css decides which buttons are on the page

whyNot.a: That's the wiring, not the walls: the page file says the button exists, and the logic makes it act.
whyNot.c: That's the walls, not the paint: styling only changes how things look, not what's there.

cards.reteach: Four trades, four jobs. The page says what's there, styling says how it looks, logic says what happens when you click, and settings hold the parts list and start commands.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
Walk your app like a house. The page is the walls: what's there. Styling is the paint: how it looks. Logic is the wiring: what happens when you click. Settings are the clipboard in the site office: the parts list.

When you find a room you don't recognise, point Claude at that one file and ask what it does in plain words.
cards.simpler: Walk your app like a house. The page is the walls: what's there. Styling is the paint: how it looks. Logic is the wiring: what happens when you click. Settings are the site clipboard: the parts list. **When you find a room you don't recognise, point Claude at that one file and ask what it does in plain words.**

cards.body:
Open your project folder in Claude Code and type: "List every file here, skipping node_modules. For each one, tell me in one line which kind it is: page, styling, logic, settings, or other (and if other, what it's for)."

Tomorrow: why that scary red error message is a gift you hand to Claude.
cards.simpler: Now **sort your own files into the 4 kinds**. Open your project folder in Claude Code and type this: "List every file here, skipping node_modules. For each one, tell me in one line which kind it is: page, styling, logic, settings, or other (and if other, what it's for)." Tomorrow: why that scary red error message is a gift you hand to Claude.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now open a project folder, name what each main file is for, and ask Claude to explain a piece you don't follow.

dubious_claims: The page file is 'usually called index.html' and holds the buttons: true for plain HTML apps, false for React/Vite apps, where index.html is a nearly empty shell.
'Most files you'll touch fall into the same 4 kinds': leaves out backend folders (e.g. convex/) and config files (vite.config, tsconfig.json) that Claude commonly creates.
repairedFrom.why: It says buttons live in index.html, but in React/Vite apps like a Convex project the buttons live in .jsx/.tsx files and index.html is nearly empty, so readers could repeat Maya's twenty-minute search in the wrong file.
repairedFrom.fix: Add one line to card 3: "If your app uses React, the walls live in .jsx or .tsx files inside src/, and index.html is just the front door." Then change exercise 2's answer text to say "the page file (index.html or a .tsx file)".
